House resumed consideration in Committee of Bill No. 36, respecting Banks and Banking.-Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance). (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
On section 91-interest which may be charged.

When the committee rose, I was going to make some observations with respect to this section. In my judgment, the section as amended by the committee is directly at variance^ with previous legislation passed by this House, and with the principle which Parliament has recognized for many years. As the amendment of the committee reads, it leaves the door wide open; the banks may charge any rate of interest. I am not going to assume that banks would do so; but I know that it has been done in some sections of the Dominion, as has been demonstrated in trials of important cases in the Supreme Court, notably that of Barretts vs. the Bank of Commrrce, a Yukon case. The bank there charged as high as twenty-four per cent on loans and renewals. It was held in that case that where the party had voluntarily paid the amount, he could not recover the excess beyond the seven per cent. We have on the statute-book of Canada the Money Lenders' Act, chapter 122 of the Revised Statutes. Section 6 reads as follows:
Notwithstanding the provisions of the Interest Act, no money-lender shall stipulate for, allow or exact on any negotiable instrument, contract or agreement, concerning a loan of

money, the principal of which is under five hundred dollars, a rate of interest or discount greater than twelve per centum per annum ; and the said rate of interest shall ba reduced to the rate of five per centum per annum from the date of judgment in any suit, action or other proceeding for the recovery of the amount due.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Has my hon. friend had
his attention called to the definition of money-lender there?

Yes, hut that was a principle which was adopted by this Parliament. It' was recognized that certain individuals should be restrained. Seeing that it has been demonstrated in the courts of the country that banks have been offenders in this respect and that they have charged as high as twenty-four per cent, this Parliament should put some restriction upon them. My proposition would he to restore the section as it was originally. I would make the rate even higher, if seven per cent is not sufficient. I would have a maximum rate of a certain amount beyond which the banks could not go, that is, that they could not accept or retain any rate beyond that. Of course that would not apply in cases where the interest did not exceed one dollar. Section 4 of the Money Lenders' Act reads:
This Act shall not apply to any loan or' transaction in which the whole interest or discount charged or collected in connection therewith does not exceed the sum of fifty cents.
I would say: 'the sum of one dollar.' Where the bank did accept or retain, even with the consent of the party who secured the loan, the excess amount beyond the limitation which we had fixed, it should be recoverable in any court of competent jurisdiction. I would also have a provision that each bank shall furnish a statement monthly to the Minister of Finance showing the maximum and minimum rates of interest or discount charged or retained on loans by such bank at its head office or at any of its branch offices, such statement not to include percentage rates or minimum charges on small loans less than fifty dollars. That would seem to obviate one difficulty with respect to a bank showing a very high rate of interest on a loan of say twenty dollars for a month, where it had charged its minimum charge of fifty or seventy-five cents or a dollar, as the case might be. I would not require banks to make statements as to such small loans; but, if we fixed for them a rate of interest beyond which they must not go, then we should tie them down so that they shall be obliged to return any excess, if the party brings suit against them in any court of competent jurisdiction. Seven per cent ' as a maximum amount is perhaps too small under present conditions. I do not think
327i
banks in the East usually go beyond that; but, in the West they charge as much as-eight or twelve per cent, and in this case from the Yukon, they charged a rate as high as twenty-four per cent. Tinder those circumstances I think we should limit the rate to perhaps 8 ner cent, the 8 per cent not to apply to small loans in regard to which a minimum charge is made by the bank. I think if you make the maximum rate higher, the banka, should be obliged to refund any excess of that charge, providing the borrower seeks it. In addition to that I would require that this statement be made to the minister monthly, so that publicity should be given as to the minimum and maximum rates charged by the banks of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend propose to offer an amendment?
I was going to propose an amendment with respect to the monthly statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it would be a
mistake to raise the rate-of interest from 7 per cent to 8 per cent, even if we made the 8 per cent absolute. In those districts of Canada in which the prevailing rate is now less than 8 per cent, there would be a tendency on the part of the banks to feel a justification that they do not now feel in raising the rate to1 8 per cent. I am impressed with the suggestion put forward in the committee that the provision for a 7 per cent rate is an indication to the banks on the part of Parliament, notwithstanding the decision of the Privy Council, that the rates of interest should be moderate, bo far as the coast communities are concerned, in which the rates of interest are at present 7 per cent or under, I think the fixing of the rate at 8 per cent would have an adverse influence. Let us take the case of a western community, particularly those parts of the country in which a higher rate than 8 per cent prevails. It was shown to the satisfaction of the committee that the bankers discriminate as to loans; they always have and always will. A gets a better rate than B, because his account is larger, his credit better or his standing higher in the community. A borrower in a particular community where the deposits are large and where there is particularly keen competition will receive more favourable rates than a borrower in a community where there are no depositors, where the deposits are small, or where there is no competition on the part of the banks. The hon. member has mentioned the case of the Yukon. I have no hesitation in saying that if you had had an 8 per cent or 9 per cent maximum rate in the Yukon, fixed by the Bank Act, the business community of that territory would

EQt have received any banking accommodation at all, because the carrying on of the banking business would not have paid. I do not believe that it is feasible to impose legislation that would compel the banks to make loans in any particular community. The banks, so far as the Yukon is concerned at the time of the gold rush, would not have entered the field at all if they had been limited to an 8 per cent or 9 per cent rate. I know that there prevails in _ the community in general a very considerable sentiment in favour of strictly limiting the rates of interest, but I submit that we must face all the conditions that exist in such a large country as Canada. As legislators, it is our duty to do what we regard to be the proper thing in the interests of the community as a whole, and I am perfectly satisfied that any legislation, so far as western communities are concerned, seeking strictly to limit the rate of interest to eight per cent would defeat the very purpose of those who are desirous of bringing about that condition. I think that banking accommodation would be denied to a large number of borrowers who would be willing to pay eight per cent or ten per cent, especially upon small loans, to their own great advantage. I think that view was amply confirmed by evidence that was taken before the committee. We are all in sympathy with the principle of obtaining as low a rate of interest as we can for the borrowing community, but two things must be borne in mind. In the first place, banking, just like any other business, is engaged in for purposes of gain, and, so long as there is no combination affecting the rates of interest there is, undoubtedly, competition, not only among banks, but between the banks and private lenders of money, for there is a great deal of money loaned in the country by institutions other than the chartered and private banks. It is desirable that bank captial should flow into this country, and if we adopt a rate of discount which will affect or restrict the profits of the bank unduly, I think the whole country would feel the ill-effects of it, because the money would simply cease to flew into that capital. Undoubtedly you will injure the borrowing community if you adopt restrictions that might be too harsh. Evidence was given by the manager of the Weyburn Bank, who produced a statement with regard to his institution-a very carefully managed bank, at least so far as we oould judge. It was a bank operating in Saskatchewan, a purely western institution not doing any business in the East at all. His evidence was confirmed by figures which he laid before the committee as to the net earnings Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
of the bank and the rates of discount charged, and it was clearly shown to the satisfaction of the committee that a reduction to seven per cent of the rate of interest which they obtained upon loans would close the doors of the bank. During the course of his examination, I asked him:
Q. I want you to make a little calculation for me. According to the bank statement your current loans and discounts amount to $894,000?-A. Did you take in the past due?
The Chairman.-It is about $910,000.
The Witness.-About $910,000.
By Hon. Mr. White:
Q. How much interest would you lose on these if they were on a 7 per cent basis? What is your average?-A. I would say our average is 9 per cent.
Q. Then you would lose 2 per cent?-A.
Q. What is 2 per cent on $900,000?-A. $18,000.
Q. How much per cent is that on your capital?-A. About 6 per cent.
Q. How much dividend do you pay?-A. 5 per cent, well, now we make more than that.
Q. If a 2 per cent reduction in interest were made, what in your opinion, would be the effect?-A. It would wipe out our profit on the loaning business. You might as well go out of the banking business.
Here is a man who gave his evidence very sincerely and impressively before that committee, and I think it establishes the fact that so far as the hanking business in the western community is concerned by banks operating there solely-and that is a fair test-having regard to the amount of deposits that they can get now at any rate 

I look forward to a great increase in deposits there, because I have the greatest faith in the West-to compel the banks to limit their interests to seven per cent would defeat the very purpose that hon. gentlemen have in view who advocate that course. I understand that my hon. friend from Westmorland does not differ on that point. There was a suggestion made in the committee, I think by my hon. friend from Westmorland and concurred in by myself and many other members of the committee, and I think favourably received by the committee, though there was some difficulties that arose or were suggested as likely to arise in its carrying out because of difficulty in obtaining returns to comply with the requirements of the amendment. I agreed in principle with the amendment that was suggested, for this reason, that I believe that the best result will be obtained by not limiting the rate of interest, and it will not be limited when we restore that section 91, because as I pointed out before the House rose, the decision under that section enables the bank to charge such rate of interest as may be agreed upon, provided it is taken at the time the loan is made and is not recovered

by legal protest. I believe that it is better to leave the situation exactly as it is. But I am a great believer, as are many other members of both sides of the House- in fact, I have no doubt, all members on both sides, because we are legislators-in publicity as a check upon anything that might be against the interests of the community. Therefore, I suggested as an amendment to the amendment in the committee-or I am not sure that I suggested it to the committee, but I had it drafted- that a return should be made by the banks at least once a year-because there is great difficulty in making returns monthly- whereby the maximum rate of interest charged by the banks throughout Canada should be made a subject of return to the Finance Department, so that if an extortionate rate of interest were being charged, the bank could be asked why it was necessary to charge this rate, what the circumstances are which made necessary a rate so much in excess of the rate mentioned in the Bank Act as being fair. Therefore, I shall propose an amendment to section 91, though I have only been able to consider it very cursorily, because it has been comparatively hurriedly drafted by'my assistant deputy who has been a good legal advisor throughout this Bill as all the members of the committee know. The amendment is as follows:
The hank shall make a quarterly return-*
Because that will give them time.
-to the. minister as of the last juridical day of the months of March, June, September and December in each year, giving such particulars as will be prescribed by regulations made by the Treasury Board of the interest and discount rates charged by the bank.
I have it in mind that the Treasury Board can make regulations as to loans up to a certain amount, loans in certain districts and so on, so that it would not be of a general character and yet would be fair to the banks. Sub-section 3 is also a part of the amendment:
Such returns shall be made up and sent in within the first thirty days of the respective last juridical days aforesaid, and shall be signed by the same persons as are required to sign the monthly returns made to the minister under section 112 of this Act.
The effect of section 91 on the amendment will be that the banks will be reluctant to go into new districts and get such a rate of interest as they may be able to get, and that may be fair having regard to the conditions. On the other hand, they would be compelled to make a return to the Finance Department so that, if it should appear that an undue advantage is taken of the borrowing community, attention would be drawn to it and the matter may be taken up between the department and the
bank. It seems to me this is as good a reason as we can get on this question.

I am very thoroughly in accord with the suggestion made by the Minister of Finance. Bearing in mind the fact that the minister has made provision for a return to be given in the month of January as to the value of bank premises, I was going to suggest the following:
All banks shall furnish a statement on the first day of January in each year to the minister showing the maximum and minimum rates of interest or discount paid to, charged or retained by such bank at its head office or at any of its branch offices during the preceding year on loans-this not to apply to any loan or transaction in which the whole interest or discount charged or collected in connection therewith does not exceed the sum of one dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would point out to my hon. friend that the provision for regulations of the Treasury Board, I think, cover the situation better than his amendment, as giving more flexibility.

I had accepted the suggested amendment of the hon. minister. I was going to explain to him that I had in mind offering this amendment for the consideration of the committee. But, in view of the step the minister has taken, I will certainly not interject my amendment.
Would the minister say what amendment is before the committee? I understood him to move an amendment before dinner, another was suggested and the minister has moved another one still.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend has before him, no doubt, the Bill as it came from the committee. I propose to strike out section 91 as it appears in the Bill and to restore section 91 as it exists in the present Act. Again, there is the amendment which I have just suggested with regard to returns concerning rates of interest and discount.

I think the minister is right in restoring section 91 to the Bill. It is pretty hard to regulate what a man shall charge for his money. Although I know the banks are recipients of very great favours at the hands of Parliament, yet I presume that there are cases in which they might have the right to charge more than in other cases, although I must say I can hardly follow the argument that it costs two per cent more to do business in the West than in the East. It may be true; I am not an authority. I wanted to say a word on behalf of the banks. I do not think they have ever been guilty of usury so far as the eastern portion of Canada is concerned;

at least I have never known of a case. I have never known of a bank in eastern Canada asking for more than seven per cent interest during the last ten or twelve years, [DOT]although it may be possible that they have *done so. I know that a very large amount of money is loaned at six per cent, but so Jar as our portion of Canada is concerned, 1 do not think there is very much fault to find with the amount of interest charged by the banks. I think it would be better to leave that seven per cent in the Act. While the minister does not think it is of much legal value, and probably, in view of the decision of the Privy Council, it is not, I would rather see it left that way than have a maximum of eight per cent provided,_ for I fear that if we fix the maximum at eight per cent, in many cases the banks would say, if we are compelled to do business fpr less than it costs us in the West we will have to make it up in the East, and probably the borrowers in the East would suffer. Between the two evils I would choose the least, and therefore I think it would be better to leave the section as it was *originally.

I am very
[DOT]sorry to take up any of the time of the [DOT]committee on a matter which has been -discussed so much, but I have certain opinions which I voiced on the second Teading, and which I feel impelled to repeat now. Throughout my life, ever since I could do any thinking, I have considered that it-was a misfortune to have any law upon the statute book of a civilized country which was not respected and enforced, I do not care against wrhat class of society that law is directed, or against what proceeding of society. Now the original clause reads in part:
The bank may take any interest not exceeding seven per cent, but no higher rate of interest shall be recoverable by the bank.
If that clause has any object, it is to assert that the law of Canada, as applied to banks, is that they shall get seven per cent interest upon money as the maximum. What are the facts, Mr. Chairman? In the province of Alberta, if a man goes to the bank, it is not a case of collecting interest before hand; he is presented with a note. If his credit is good his own name will be accepted on the note, if not, he is required to have the signature of another citizen of xepute. On that note he promises to pay eight per cent, and the banks invariably collect that eight per cent. I say it is a misfortune that in a country in the British Empire we should, with our eyes open, enact this clause and have this proceeding go on. I do not wonder that a^ lawyer of the eminence and repute of Chief Justice Moulton should have given the decision he [DOT]did, because by that decision I think he
Mr. CARVELL.
inferentially expressed his absolute contempt for that clause as a piece of legislation. I have not his private opinion, but I am perfectly certain that if I got it, it would be what I am expressing at the nre-sent moment. I would he surprised if it were otherwise. I do not know what answer my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and other hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House may make to what I am stating. It may be said that when a man signs a note at the bank to pay interest of eight per cent in six months, he does so with eyes open, and makes a contract. I quite agree, but he cannot help himself. He needs the money. The point is that the law of the land says that you shall not take more than seven , per cent, and the banks proceed incontinently to take eight per cent. I do not know how this assembly can respect itself if it knows the facts and enacts this clause. I can only explain the fact that more borrowers do not take advantage of this clause on two grounds. One may be that they do not know anything about the clause, and I think that is true of the great majority of them. The other may be that they are so upright, that when they sign a contract they feel like standing by it. Suppose the latter is the explanation. It would be so in my own case; no man can be surer of another man's uprightness than he can be of his own. Suppose the latter explanation is the true one, what conclusion must we draw? Why, it is that the morality of the ordinary borrower in the province of Alberta is higher than that of the Parliament of Canada, because Parliament enacts a clause which extends an invitation to financial immorality on the part of the borrower, who can sign a note saying:	I
promise to pay eight per cent but who, if __ he knows enough, may say at the end of six months, you can whistle for your eight per cent for all you are going to get is seven per cent. If Mr. Justice Moulton had a poor opinion of the original clause,
I would not like to think what his opinion would be of the amendment. But as the minister has dropped it, I do not want to criticise it. I never lick a dead foal. I do not favour any clause, I could not favour any clause, -Which says that the banks cannot take more than seven per cent and which yet allows them to take eight per cent. I could not do that and respect my intelligence and common sense. I hope the minister and the committee understand where I am at. I am certain that the people of Alberta do. One thing the people of Alberta do not understand is why they should pay eight per cent while the people of Saskatchewan pay only seven per cent. But if he cannot make better legislation, I suppose we will have to go on paying the extra one per cent.

I agree with what the
hon. member for Red Deer has said, and I suggest to the Minister of Finance that every argument he used in favour of the clause as he proposed to have it, was an argument that there should be no clause at all. I quite agree with the hon. member for Red Deer that if the clause in regard to interest is not to be respected, it should not be there.
It should be penal.
What I urge is what was urged by my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) and by other members, that whatever may be considered as a maximum rate of interest should be fixed as the maximum.

What
is the hon. member's suggestion?
I am not making a suggestion at the moment; it is not my business.
You represent the West.

Let my hon. friend represent North Ontario a little more honestly than he does, and it will be better for North Ontario and for the rest of us. All I want to say is that if a purely western bank, such as the Weyburn Bank, can do business, and does do business, on an average rate of interest of nine per cent, there is either nothing in the contention that our system of banking with branches all over the country is superior, or else the system is not being carried out fairly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Might I call my hon.
friend's attention to the fact that the Weyburn Bank's rates were eight per cent, ten per cent and twelve per cent, but the average was nine per cent?

The Weyburn Bank is a purely western bank, dependent on western capital and western deposits, but its average rate of interest was nine per cent. That is to say if the Weyburn Bank charged all its customers nine per cent, it would get just the same revenue as it gets to-day. It suits the Weyburn Bank, being an American institution, run by people from the United States, according to United States principles, to vary their rate of interest. The average rate is nine per cent. If the Weyburn bank, depending entirely on western capital and on western business, can do business at nine per cent, our chartered banks having their headquarters in the East ought to be able to do business in western Canada at a lower rate than nine per cent. If they are not, there is no benefit in the system of branch banks. My hon. friend seems to think that it is a
splendid arrangement whereby there is to be left on the face of the Act a provision, as he says, suggesting to the banks that they ought not to charge more than seven per cent but at the same time leaving them free to charge whatever they please. He says that will work beautifully because in eastern Canada they will only charge seven per cent and in western Canada they may charge whatever they want to. If my hon. friend will take the section out of the Act altogether and will hold out to the country that his Bank Act, put through Parliament this year of grace, 1913, takes no account of the crime of usury when practised by a bank upon the western people, he will be honest anyway in his legislation. But to put a section in the Act which holds out to western, as well as eastern, people, the idea that the banks are limited to a charge of seven per cent and yet allows them to charge what they like is not honest legislation, it is not fair and it is not decent, and I protest against it and protest very strongly. My hon. friend made the suggestion that a fixed rate of seven per cent would close the banks operating in the West.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said that in the case of the Weyburn bank the manager showed that it would, but that in regard to other banks, my view was that they would not go into new districts to the same extent as they otherwise would and that probably they would draw out from some that they are now in.

Precisely. Neither myself nor my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle, nor any of the men from the West, urged that the rate be limited to seven per cent. What we are asking to be protected against is the usurious rates which are being charged, which my hon. friend knows are being charged and which he cannot justify.. My hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin) stated to this House that in the course of his business he had collected accounts for banks where the interest was twelve per cent. It is nothing more nor less than a scandal, .and it should not be permitted under the legislation of this Parliament. It is a disgrace to the banking system of Canada. We know that the reputable banks of Canada do not do that sort of business, but there are some banks which are run in that way, they are doing that kind of business, they are doing it in the West, and my hon. friend stands up and says that it is all right so long as they do it in the WeiSt. I object most strenuously to that proposition. I do not ask that a low maximum rate be fixed, but let us have protection against usury in the West under the provisions of this Act, or else let my hon. friend say that he _ will not , give any protection and that, while other

institutions and persons are prevented from practising usury, the 'banks shall have free and full liberty to do it so long as they do it west of lake Superior.

When this matter came
before the Banking and Commerce Committee, we found ourselves confronted with this difficulty. The law, as it stood in the old Act, was made up of the original section plus a decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the net result of which was that if a bank took their charge by way of discount they were entitled to charge any amount they cared to levy, but if they did not make the charge by way of discount but by way of interest, they were not entitled to charge an amount in excess of seven per cent. If the instrument called for the payment of a rate of interest in excess of seven per cent it was ultra vires as to any rate in excess of the legal rate of five per cent. Part of the law was not exactly as the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) has stated. It was this: If the rate of interest was in excess of seven per cent the borrower had a right to say: ' I will- pay five per cent/ and the banks could not collect beyond that amount. In the consideration of the situation considerable evidence was given by western representatives and, if I remember correctly, one Mr. Chipman gave evidence and produced some two hundred or three hundred notes of various banks by which he amply proved that the ordinary rate of interest in the West did not, except in odd cases, exceed ten per cent. Further evidence was given by Mr. Henderson, representing the Bankers' Association, by which he showed that the expense of carrying on business in the West was 2-58 per cent higher than in the East, and that the average rate of increase in interest was two and a half per cent in the West as compared with the rate in the East. He read extracts from the statements of various men in authority who went the length of saying that if this Parliament tried to fix a rate of interest of less than seven per cent the net result would be that the supply of money to the West would be restricted and there would be a dearth. The committee therefore found itself confronted by these difficulties. If they fixed a rate of seven per cent, or less, then the West was going to suffer from the closing up of branch banks because the cost of doing a small business was necessarily proportionately larger in the West than that of doing a larger business in the East. There were no deposits there and nothing like the proportion of loans made by the banks as compared with the amount of business done in the East. The net result was that section 91 as it stands in the Bill as presented to Mr. OLIVER.
the House to-day was drafted and carried in the committee, togetner with a subsection that monthly the banks must present to the Minister of Finance a statement showing what the rate of interest was on all loans of over one hundred dollars. The committee in dealing with section 91, drafted as it appears in the Act now under consideration, together with this sub-section, thought they would effectively block any attempt on the part of any bank to charge usurious rates. But the committee, at a subsequent sitting, cancelled the sub-section, and left section 91 as it appears in the Bill now before the committee. Under the present clause a bank may collect by way of discount any rate it pleases, but in case it charges a higher rate of interest than seven per cent, it can collect only seven per cent. It differs from the original section in the old Act in this, that a rate of seven per cent could not be collected if a rate in excess of this were charged as interest, but only a rate of five per cent. 1 quite agree with the opinion of the hon. member for Red Deer that it is most unfortunate that this Parliament should enact a law that practically means nothing. I am with him in this, that whatever we intend to be the law, we should state clearly and fully and that we should if necessary put in some penalty to insure that the provision shall be observed. J am sorry to say that I do not agree with my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in thinking the old section better than the present. It seems to me that the wisest provision we could make	is not to restore the
-old section, but to leave the present section 91 as ia the reprinted Bill, and put in an amendment or sub-section to the effect that monthly or quarterly returns of all loans over one hundred dollars shall be made to the minister. The publicity incidental to that notice would prevent, through shame, usurious rates, and section 91 in the amended Bill is consistent with the intention of the committee.

There was evidence produced in the Banking Committee to show that it costs two per cent more to conduct banking business in the West than in the East and consequently the banks insisted on the privilege of charging nine per cent. According to that, any rate beyond seven per cent in the East is too high and should not be permitted. In Nova Scotia some branch banks are charging eight per cent for loans, a fact which cannot be denied. They are not doing it in cities and the larger towns where there are two or three banks doing business, but I do know they are charging eight per cent in certain places in Nova Scotia where they have bought out the competing banks and have a mo-

nopoly. If it was the intention of this Parliament when the Bank Act was revised in 1901 that banks should absolutely be debarred from charging more than seven per cent, and if it turns out that a flaw has been discovered, as indicated by the decision of the Privy Council, and that banks are permitted to charge more than seven per cent, it is our duty to so amend the existing section of the Act that the courts cannot get around the intention of Parliament. Surely language can be found to explain definitely what the intention of Parliament is, so that there will be no danger of a decision of the Privy Council or any other court giving a different interpretation to the clause.
The financial conditions existing in the West and in the Yukon were more pressing in 1901 when the Bank Act was last revised than they are to-day, and with, a full knowledge of these conditions as regards the high cost of money in the West and in the Yukon, Parliament deliberately asserted that banks should not have the right to charge more than seven per cent. Therefore, I think the situation existing in the West to-day is not such as to induce Parliament to modify the Act in this particular. My hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) points out that unless the banks charge their interest by way of discount, and deduct it from the proceeds of the note, by agreement forced upon the borrower, they could not charge more than seven per cent. I know that banks will be sure to take advantage of the interpretation of the statute that will enable them to collect the highest amount of interest by way of discount. There is not much danger that a bank manager will permit the borrower to place upon the face of the note the rate of interest he is paying, but rather he will discount the note and collect his discount before he passes the balance over to the borrower. My hon. friend from Kingston says that if that note runs beyond the time for which a higher rate of interest than seven per cent is mentioned, the higher rate cannot be collected. In the West, as I understand the hon. member for Red Deer, banks advance money upon a note signed by the maker without requiring an endorser when the maker is in good financial standing. That practice does not prevail in Nova Scotia. It is absolutely impossible for the maker of a note, no matter how wealthy he may be and how good his financial standing is, to get a loan of five dollars unless he has an endorser.
Oh, no.

I am speaking now of the
smaller communities. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) may have had a different experience.
And in pretty big communities too.

I quite agree with what
has been stated by the hon. member (Mr. Kyte), that it is better to restore the clause as it was and as it does exist in the present Act.
I was going to add also: in view of the amendment proposed by the Minister of Finance, which I think further strengthens it.

My reason for saying so
is that the section as it now exists suggests seven per cent to the country as a reasonable rate of interest generally. I think it would be improper to increase that suggested rate of interest because it would give an indication to the country that this House of Commons thought a larger rate of interest would be reasonable. The next reason why I think it should be retained just as it is in the present Act is because it has	been	there	for a long
time; it has	become honoured in
usage, and there has been no general outcry in the country against it. I think, in the way in which it has been generally exercised, it has proved satisfactory to the country, although it may not have proved satisfactory to some customers. The third reason is because it has received judicial interpretation. I think that recent judicial interpretation shows clearly the exact meaning of that section, which is this, that if the parties [DOT] agree upon a rate of interest and it is paid, at once it becomes a settled and closed account; a person who does so pay does it voluntarily with eyes open, knowing what is being done. The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) says: They usually cannot help themselves. I submit that the customer is in no worse a position than if a fixed rate of interest was put in the Act, say seven or eight per cent, because the bank would decide not to lend in that particular district at that rate and so the customer would"not get the benefit. Therefore it seems to me, when it is left as a matter of agreement, and people ordinarily understand how to protect themselves, it is the more reasonable way of doing it. If the payment is left executory, that is, if the agreement is simply that the interest is to be paid, then the Bank must stick to the seven per cent, because otherwise it would be an illegal agreement and then the only interest that could be charged would be five per cent. Under these circumstances I quite agree with the hon. minister that the old section should be retained, and I also agree with him in respect to the rider that should be attached to it.

I just want to call the attention of my hon. friend to the way in which this section, which has been found so useful, has operated in the past. I Mr. KYTE.
have here a statement of the proceedings of the Banking and Commerce Committee which sets out that the Bank of British North America has placed certain loans. There are thirty or forty of them and none of them at a late less than ten per cent. The rates charged by the Dominion Bank vary from eight to eleven per cent; by the Canadian Bank-of Commerce, from eight to twelve per cent; by the Union Bank, from eight to twelve per cent; by the Merchants' Bank, from eight to twelve per cent; by the Northern Crown Bank, from eight to twelve per cent; by the Bank of Hamilton, from eight to twelve per cent; by the Weybum Bank, from eight to ten to twelve per cent; by the Bank of Toronto from eight to ten per cent; by the Quebec Bank, from nine to ten per cent; by the Bank of Ottawa, from eight to twelve per cent. The rate charged by the Royal Bank stands at eight per cent. In view of this evidence before the committee as to the regard that has been paid to that section of the Act, unless the hon. minister is going to make the section have some effect, the proper course would be to strike it out. It has discredited our legislation, or it has discredited our administration, because no regard has apparently been paid to it. I certainly think that such legislation shovdd not remain on the Statute Book unless the Government is prepared to say that the interests of the people are to be protected by the intent of that section being carried out.

Which section do you
mean, the old or the new?

I mean that neither of
them should remain. The new section has the merit of being honest. It simply authorizes the banks to practice usury without restriction. That is honest and fair, but I object to it. I do not think it would be for the credit of Parliament to allow such a section as that to pass into permanent legislation. As for the old section, while on its face it has an appearance of value, as a matter of fact, on the word of the minister and on the evidence before the committee, it has no value. It is not the intention of the minister to give it value. Therefore, I say it should not appear on the statute-book. The business of Parliament and of the Government is to provide in this Act against the charging of usurious rates of interest by a bank.

I have not yet heard this evening from any hon. member a sound reason for departing from the section as we find it in the reprinted Bill. All the hon. gentlemen who have suggested that we revert to the section in the Bill as originally introduced have not accompanied their remarks with any argument, any reasoning, any logic, which appeals to me in the

slightest degree. I quite agree with the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that Parliament should say what it means and should mean what it savs. There are many difficulties in the way, and I quite easily perceive motives which may prompt hon. gentlemen to suggest the restoration of the old section. At the same time, I feel that the people of this country would be better satisfied if the section in the Bill as reprinted were left and were enacted as our final judgment rather than if we were to restore the old section which reallv means nothing, and which I do not think has any value by reason of the judicial interpretation given to it by the Supreme Court of Canada, because I believe that, in view of the judgment o'f the Privy, Council in the McHugh case, on the first occasion when the section of the old Bill ever reaches the Privy Council for internre-tation they would decide that the Canadian banks could not recover more than seven per cent even by taking that rate of interest either at the time of discount or at any other time.

That was a
decision of the Privy Council.

No, they have not so
decided. That question did not come up in the McHugh case at all.
I believe the rate of interest, with the competition we have in this country, will adjust itself usually to the proper rate. Neither our friends in the West nor people in the East can expect cheap money and high priced land, or cheap money and high priced other commodities. Whether my hon. friend from Bed Deer would believe me to be a free trader or not. in the matter of money I am at one with him; and I would prefer very much, though it is a matter of indifference to me personally, that we should leave the section in the reprinted Bill as it is.

Does the hon. gentleman
know the rate charged by the banks in the city of Halifax?

I suppose it is seven
or' eight per cent at the present time, and that on small notes of $25 or $50 the rates would be higher. I do not blame a bank for charging more than seven per cent in such eases.
My information is that the banks are charging eight per cent in communities which have only one bank.

There is no clause to which the committee gave more serious attention than the one under discussion. We received evidence from many quarters and endeavoured to assimilate that evidence. I concur wholly with what the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has
said, that the clause really should remain in the Bill. While I agree with the hon. member for Bed Deer that we should not put legislation on our statute-book that is not to be carried out, still I think that this clause is such that it can be carried out. That is my view. It should be carried out in the spirit which the Finance Minister intended it should be, that is that the rates contracted for in the first place shall be the amount collected and if the note becomes the subject of a process of law for collection, the interest shall not be greater than seven per cent. That is perfectly practical legislation, and while there is no penalty attached to the breaking of it, still the plain statement the Minister of Finance has given as to what he wishes the hanks to understand to be the law, I think, will correct any overcharge in the long run, if such there be. The hon. member for Edmonton I think could hardly be sincere when he says that bank interest should be uniform throughout Canada.
No, I did not say any such thing.
The hon. member objected that the West is paying more than the East.

I say that the West is
certainly paying more than the East, but I did not say we were legislating to compel it to pay more than the East. What I said was that I wanted legislation to prevent usurious rates of interest in the West.

The tenor of the
hon. gentleman's remarks was that the East was exacting more interest from the West than was legitimate.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, I will not submit to being put in a position of segregating West and East. It was the Finance Minister who pointed out the necessity of charging-more in the West than in the East.
Mr, COCBSHUTT:	I do not wish to
misrepresent my hon. friend. I understood that to be the basis of his argument. I want to point out that there are sections even in his own province that on a business basis should be charged more than others. My hon. friend will not deny it.
I do not denjr_ it. To make it clear I may say that irf^Edmonton, I think they charge no more than one per cent more than in Toronto and perhaps not any more.

There are whole
districts in which new towns are just established, where immediate success is doubtful and where the business trans-

acted is very limited. It is not reasonable to expect that a bank will go into such a district and lend money at the same rate as in a settled community. The bankers who gave evidence before the committee made it clear that they should not take up business on that basis. They would not go into a new community and take the risk of the expense in order to do business there and charge the same rates of interest as in a community in one of the established parts of Canada. It is not only in the West that high interest rates are charged. In the clay belt-which I believe the hon. gentleman spoke of as a myth-just as high rates are charged. The new districts whether East or West must pay relatively high rates of interest, which is perfectly right. I have no brief to speak' foT the banks, but let me give to my hon. friend the statement of the manager of the bank at Weyburn, who, I think, he will accept as an authority on such a matter. This manager was asked whether similar credit was any better in the. United States than in Canada, whether banking facilities were better and money cheaper. His reply was to the effect that where a man in Saskatchewan or Alberta could borrow two thousand dollars at nine per cent, in the western states similarly situated he could only get one thousand dollars at twelve per cent, if we are to compare ourselves with others across the line -and the hon. gentleman has often been anxious to make such a comparison-we have the evidence of this bank manager at Weyburn that a man in Canada would get double the amount at twenty-five per cent less interest than one similarly situated in the United States. That shows that our banks are reasonable. I would point out to the committee that if you are going to put too much limitation on banks, if you are going to reduce their credits, you are going to make it more difficult to get capital into banking institutions. You cannot encourage capital to go into banking institutions with a club. The only thing to be done is to make the revenue so inviting that it will tempt the investment of capital. The evidence given to the committee shows that the return on banking capital in Canada, so far as the shareholders are concerned, is less than five and a half per cent, and in addition to that they have the double liability. Surely, nobody will say that when the profits of the shareholders are less than five and a half per cent, with a double liability, the banks are overcharging the people. I think that the Finance Minister has in that clause a very wise provision. I agree with the hon. junior member for Halifax that it is better to keep the present wording, be-Mr. COCKSHUTT.
cause it is the result of mature thought, and I believe that it will justify itself in the working out. I trust that before the committee reverts to the old clause they will consider the wording we have here, believing that it will work out to the advantage of both East and West, North and South. Before I sit down, let me say I believe this country is fortunate in that it has in the financial chair of this House a gentleman of the experience of the Hon. Mr. White. He has been a man among a million on this measure, both in his patience and in the wisdom and tact he has brought to bear upon this Bill. The more closely you follow what he has laid out, I believe, the nearer you will be to promoting the general advantage of Canada through this measure.
Mr. BENNETT (Calgary: It is a very simple question that is before the committee: Shall or shall not Parliament impose a restriction on the rate of interest the banks may charge ? That question has been solved in two ways. By the late Parliament it was solved by a section which -was a gold brick.
This section proposes to make perfectly certain what we are going to do. An excellent argument may be advanced to this committee why we should not limit the rate of interest which the bank charges its customer. I am not going to discuss that at the present moment further than to say that I think there should be a restriction. As to what this first section under the old Act means, I do not think Parliament had any knowledge as to that when they passed it. When Parliament passed that section it was intended unquestionably to impose a restriction upon the rate of interest the banks should take from their customers, and it was intended that fire rate should be seven per cent. As a matter of fact, the courts in the province of British Columbia in a Rossland case, which was decided many years ago, held that a bank might discount a bill which came into its hands at any rate of interest it pleased, and so long as the customer paid that rate of interest, he could not recover it back again. When a man goes to a bank to get a note discounted, he usually wants the money so badly that he is not going to inquire whether the rate of interest is eight per cent or ten per cent; he usually pays just what the bank charges him. There was a certain case decided by the Privy Council in February of this year, and my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) cannot have read it, or if he has read it, he has not understood it, because the judgment distinctly decides that if a customer goes to a bank and discounts his note, and the bank takes

the discount and treats it as nart of its profits, customer cannot recover it back under any circumstances. These are the words of the judgment of the Privy Council in that regard:
The plaintiff must be taken to have known that the bank had no right to stipulate for and no power to recover interest at eight per cent, but he voluntarily assented to that which was equivalent to payment of interest at that rate, and he has no right to recover back any excess which he thus voluntarily paid.
The customer is estopped, by reason of his conduct, from recovering the difference between seven per cent and the rate of interest which the bank takes from him in discounting his paper. The second point decided ini that case was that as in the 'contract between the bank and its customer, contained in one of the paragraphs of a chattel mortgage, the rate reserved was eight per cent, which was one per cent in excess of the sum stipulated by the Bank Act, the bank could not recover either eight or seven per cent, but was thrown hack upon the rate usually paid when no rate of interest is stipulated, five per cent. In other words, the contract to pay eight per cent was illegal, and, being illegal, the customer was entitled to recover only five per cent. The facts of the case were these:	Large
ranchers were carrying on business; they had dealings from time to time with the bank, and paid eight, nine, and in one case ten per cent interest for their money. Their account had continued for a period of not less than ten years, and suddenly they brought an action against the bank, claiming that the accounts of the bank were incorrectly kept, that the rate of interest charged was in excess of the amount provided for by the law, and that they were entitled to an order for an accounting and for a rectification of the accounts between them. The court held that they had a right to the correction of what you might call arithmetical computations and the right to have the accounts rectified so far as the dealings between the two parties were concerned. But in a chattel mortgage given by these customers to the bank for their indebtedness, there was a statement that the rate of interest should be eight per cent, and on that state of facts the Privy Council held that the bank could only recover five per cent, because any contract with the bank, whether by way of chattel mortgage, note or other security, providing for a rate of interest in excess of eight per cent was illegal, and the bank was driven to resort to the statutory allowance of five per cent. If seven per cent had been inserted in the document as the rate of interest, it would have been all right, but, the rate being eight per cent, the contract was illegal, and only
five per cent could be collected. This is the language of the judgment dealing with that matter:
The statutory provisions applicable to the case are to be found in the Bank Act, 1906, which enacts, section 91, as follows:
The bank may stipulate for, take, reserve, or exact any rate of interest or discount not exceeding seven >per centum per annum, and may receive and take in advance any such rate, but no higher rate of interest shall be recoverable by the bank.
Their Lordships are of opinion that the express ju'ovisions of the first portion of this clause rendered it ultra vires on the part of the bank to insert in the chattel mortgage of 28th May, 1907, the stipulation that interest should be payable at the rate of eight per cent, and that therefore that stipulation is inoperative. They are of opinion, therefore, that the contention on behalf of the plaintiff in this respect is right, and that the interest under that mortgage must be calculated at the rate of hve per cent per annum.
When the Banking and Commerce Committee was face to face with this consideration, what did they do? The committee had to decide whether or not we should place a restriction upon the rate the bank should recover, or whether we should leave the old section as it stood. This old section has been properly described as a golct-brick, nothing more nor less, and the new section unquestionably has the effect mentioned by the hon. member for Edmonton. It is a perfectly honest section in so far as phraseology is concerned, and it stipulates what the rate of interest may be, but it also implies that the banks may take any amount they like. As the hon. member for Edmonton has well said, this might be a usurious rate of interest, the taking of which, I think, should be prevented. I have no hesitation in saying, so far as I am personally concerned, that I do not think this is a question as between the East and the West. It is simply a auestion whether or not this Parliament shall impose a limitation or restriction upon the rate of interest the banks may charge their customers. My own personal view is that we should fix the rate at 8 per cent. I am told on excellent authority that this would work a very great hardship, and that in the Yukon, for instance, owing to the conditions there, the rates of interest could not be restricted to 8 per cent. In that district the rates were sometimes as high as 20 per c-ent, and that rate was. not regarded as high in that .part of the country as 6 per cent might be regarded here. In the Cobalt district the rate of interest is hign, and in some remote sections of the wqstem provinces new branches could not possibly open up if the rate of interest were fixed at 8 per cent. I therefore think that the committee should strike out this section in its entirety, or make some provision by which tire bank should by publicity be, if I

may use the word, shamed into charging only a reasonable rate of interest. If we cannot impose a restriction by limiting the rate to 8 per cent, let us by some method of publicity prevent those evils which are real and not imaginary, and which by thi^legislation we will give a direct incentive and inducement to become greater. However much you may argue as to the authority or influence of individual managers, it is the individual manager who has to deal with' these transactions, not the general manager at the head office. A young manager is, as a rule, anxious to make the largest passible profits in connection with a new branch; in some instances where a man has given the bank a $100 note and has received $95, he thought he was doing a very good thing, hut the rate charged was really 20 per cent. That is the reason why I think this committee should not pass this section of the Bill.

On section 64-bank circulation redemption fund:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I wish to suggest an amendment to section 64 which is of some importance. Section 64 refers to the circulation redemption fund, and members of the committee are doubtless aware that all the banks have to contribute an amount equal to five per cent of the average note circulation to that fund, which constitutes a security for the note circulation of the banks. We are providing a gold reserve against which the banks may issue notes in excess of the amount of note circulation which they may now issue against their paid-up capital and against the fifteen per cent of the paid-up capital in reserve in the emergency period. Mr. McLeod, who appeared before the committee, wrote to me about this from London, and I think he is entirely correct in his views. He says that it is not necessary for the banks to contribute five per cent in respe'ct to the note circulation which is issued against gold. In other words, it is the note circulation, which is issued against paid-up capital, and the so-called emergency circulation that should be safeguarded by the contributions of the banks. Therefore, in order to give effect to that recommendation and suggestion, which I have said is a very pertinent and good one, I move that section 64, sub-section 8, be amended by inserting, after deleting the period, after the word ' relates,' the following:
Provided, however, that in determining the average note circulation of a bank under this sub-section the daily average for each month of the amount of the bank's deposit, (if any) in the central gold reserves, which has not
been withdrawn or deemed to be withdrawn within the meaning of this Act, shall be deducted from the greatest amount of the notes of the bank in circulation at any time during the month.
That means that the banks shall contribute five per cent of the balance. As regards the note circulation secured by gold, that is absolutely secured. That leaves it precisely as it is at present so far as the constitution of the banks is concerned towards a guarantee of the note circulation of the banks. In so far as the note circulation of the banks is safeguarded dollar for dollar by gold deposited under the provisions of the new Act, it is not necessary to contribute for that.
If it had not been for the provisions of the new Act in adding to the gold security, this would not have been necessary.
