Last night we passed this item which we did not discuss at all. The hon. minister said that we could ask any questions concerning it at a future session of the committee. It would perhaps save time and a lot of questions if he would just give us a little idea of these exhibitions; what work he is carrying on; if this vote has anything to do with the vote for the Toronto exhibition; what is included in it; who is in charge of the exhibits; what are the exhibits; what success we	are	having,	and if	weare getting	any	returns	that	he	can
see directly or if they are indirect. Exhibitions properly conducted are the best advertising we can have for Canada. What are included in the exhibits-manufactured products or natural products? A few explanations would be acceptable, so that we may know what the money is for.

This special vote is confined to large internal exhibitions, and is not for exhibitions in Canada itself. There is a vote for exhibitions every year. There is in the main estimates a vote of $50,000 for the Dominion exhibition which goes from province to province in turn. There are occasionally special votes. Last year there was a vote of $100,000 towards the ioTonto National Exhibition, to pay for a building to house the exhibits of all the provinces. As I have said this vote has nothing to do with exhibitions of that kind, but it is to be confined to what we may call international exhibitions where Canada exhibits on a very large scale her natural resources and products. The first of these exhibitions was held in Stockholm in 1897. Since that time, fifteen or twenty exhibitions have been held, the last being the Festival of Empire in London. The money of this vote is largely to be for the exhibits at the International Exhibition in Ghent, in Belgium. The same man is in charge who has been in charge for many years, Colonel Hutchison, who is well qualified for the work and has a natural genius for exhibition work. A considerable sum will also be necessary for preliminary expenses in connection with the Panama Exhibition in 1915, for which we shall have to begin to get ready before the end of the present year. The Ghent Exhibition is just opening.
I hope the names of the two commissioners published are correct, Mr. Lafontaine and Mr. Plante.

Nothing has been decided on 'that point. No assistants have been sent as yet. In regard to that, the only object in sending anybody from this side was not to represent Canada but to strengthen the staff in Belgium of Frenchspeaking people.

I do not know what the particular qualifications of Mr. Lafontaine may be, but as regards Mr. Plante, if my hon. friend will appoint him, I am sure he will find in him a man most conversant with the resources of our country and quite a creditable representative of Canada. At the time we had the exhibition at Brus-sells three years ago, Canada was never so well advertised in Europe as by our exhibit there. If my hon. friend could only reproduce what we had at Brussels-and I think he could improve on that-he would confer a great benefit on this country. I must say that in Mr. Hutchinson, and his immediate staff, Mr. Hains, for instance, we have most competent officers. At Brussels, I myself visited the exposition, and it was really a matter of pride for Canadians who were present to see the enormous crowds that were struggling from morning until evening Mr. GRAHAM.
to see the exhibits of Canada. It was practically a farmers' exhibit, a representation of the life on our Canadian farms, an exhibition of our fur-bearing animals, a display of the fruits of Canada and or the products of our forests and of our mines. It was a most extraordinary fact that so many people from that wealthy country came to see what Canada had to exhibit. I am quite sure that with the literature which was distributed there, Canada derived great benefit from that exposition. I congratulate the minister on his decision to have our exhibit this year at Ghent, and I hope Mr. Hutchinson will be given a free hand, as he has had a free hand in the past, because he has a real genius for such organization. Might I suggest to the minister _ to be generous-I do not say in salaries, because I know he will pay good salaries to our officers-but to be generous in the printing of pamphlets, booklets, atlases and other literature in French. There is in Belgium, as my hon. friend knows,- a large French population, and it is from that country that we expect, more than from France, to receive immigrants. The population of Belgium, in contradistinction to that of France, increases every year. The territory of Belgium is rather limited, and there is no country in, the world where the population is so dense. They are well-to-do farmers, they have large families and they emigrate, while the French peasants do not emigrate. Especially will that be the case this year, for the new law which is being enforced in France for service in the army will make immigration more restricted than ever. From Belgium we may expect an excellent class of farmers and gardeners, and I am quite sure that if the statistics are consulted since the exhibition of Brussels, it will be found that there has been quite an increase in the immigration from Belgium into Canada. If French and Flemish literature is being distributed, it will certainly result in a numerous class of desirable immigrants.

The hon. gentleman can rest assured that no pains will be spared to make the exposition at Ghent worthy of Canada. I agree with what he says concerning Belgium. We have a certain population from Belgium in the far West-in my own province especially. These people are most thrifty and their methods of intensive farming are a revelation to us. We could not get a better class of immigrants. We have made provision for a large distribution of suitable literature.

This item is largely increased this year as compared with last. The minister gave us a general outline of what he intended to do with the money, but it would be interesting to have items of the expenditure of this $200,000, so that

we may know how he intends to expend so large an amount.

I can only say, as I have already said, that a large proportion of this money is to be spent in connection with the exposition in Ghent. That exposition will close about October or November. But before the expiry of the fiscal year, we shall have to incur fairly heavy expense in getting ready for the Panama exposition to be held at San Francisco in 1915. As my hon. friend knows, if he has seen these expositions, there is enormous expense in sending the exhibits and otherwise. I think he will find that for this expenditure, large as it is, the country will get a very excellent return in final result.
From an answer given to a question which I asked in the House some time ago, I understood that the Government did not intend to participate in the Panama Exposition.

I think my hon. friend is confusing the Panama Exposition with the San Diego Exposition. It was not thought advisable to take part in the latter, as the San Francisco Exposition is probably the more important.
Can the minister tell us to what extent Canada intends to take part in the Panama Exposition?

I could not give my
hon. friend any definite information, but speaking personally, for it is somewhat early to take the matter up officially, my own feeling is that at the Panama Exposition Canada would be justified in making one of the strongest exhibitions that she has ever made. It is of immense importance that on that occasion we should be worthily represented, and that our great natural resources should be given due prominence.
Have representations been made to the Government by the manufacturers of Canada with regard to their being represented at one of these' great expositions?
I have not any in mind.

I see no reason why the manufacturers should not endeavour to exhibit their products at these great fairs so that the people of the world would understand not only that we are a great agricultural country, but also that we have important manufacturing industries as well. I say this to impress on the manufacturers of Canada what I have often said to them privately: that they are missing a great opportunity in not coming to the front and endeavouring to get their products to these great expositions with a view to showing
the people of the world that we are a manufacturing as well as an agricultural country.
Agricultural development of dairying and fruit industries; improvement in transportation, sale and trade in fruit and other agricultural products, $190,000.

The items compos-in(r
this amount are: expenses in connection with headquarters, $15,000; expenses connected with the various dairying branches, $62,000; fruit division, $70,000; markets division, $22,790; cold -storage, $18,900; a total of $190,000 and an increase of over last year's estimates of $50,000,
What, generally speaking, are the dairying operations of the department?

We are taking up various kinds of work. One of the important activities in which we are engaged is the extension of a system of what we call dairy record centres. Under this system we plaoa an expert, who thoroughly understands the use of a Babcock test, in charge of a certain district, and whose duty it is, within a certain radius to test the cows, the products of which are going to the creameries. The results of his tests are made known among the farmers who own the herds, in order that they may be instructed in the best methods of feeding and caring for their animals, and they may be enabled to tell which animals are paying and which are not. We have now nearly twenty of these centres.
Where are these centres located?

There are nine or ten centres in various parts of the province of Ontario, and three or four in Quebec. We are establishing two or three in the maritime provinces; so far we have not gone into the western parts at all, except in one of the smaller districts of British Columbia.
In what portions of the maritime provinces have these centres been established?

In the maritime provinces we have not done very much as yet. There is a station at Clifton, New Brunswick; and we have one in Prince Edward Island, we are establishing a centre in the French Acadian portion of New Brunswick, and propose to extend the system during this, or certainly during next year.
What about Nova Scotia?

We have many of these points under consideration, so far as the expenditure which we propose

"to make to enable us to do the work this year.
Are these officers permanent? Do they remain the whole year in one locality?
The officer works the whole year round, and by using the Babcock test he is enabled to tell the farmer the exact amount of butterfat contained in the product of each cow.
Does he travel over a certain district, or is he permanently located in one place?
He works within a certain radius, sometimes within a circle of twelve, fifteen or twenty miles.

If it is the intention to establish a station in Nova Scotia, it would be desirable to have it located in the centre of the province. The hon. member referred to Yarmouth, and, while I have no objection to the establishment of one of these centres in the Yarmouth district, it is at the extreme end of the province.

I was speaking only
generally; it is not decided in what particular part of the province the centre will be located, but I know we are making arrangements to establish one in Nova Scotia.

Has any arrangement
been made for the establishment of one of these centres in the north-eastern part of the province of New Brunswick?
We are making arrangements to start work in that part of the country, I think in the county-of Kent.
That district is perhaps . the best farming portion of north-eastern New Brunswick.

It is not always advisable to start these things in the best sections. It is sometimes advisable to start them in the sections that are not so far advanced, so as to give better education to the people.
What are the prospects of am extension of this work in the prairie provinces?

I cannot answer my
hon. friend offhand. We have developed the work to a very considerable extent. We started four or five years ago with two centres I think, and we have gradually developed until we have seventeen or eighteen. It is quite obvious that we cannot extend the work to every portion of the country, otherwise we would commit ourselves to an enormous expenditure. The result of the work has -been so satisfactory that whereas one firm which had been Mr. BURRELL.
in the habit of selling fifty Babcock testers three years ago, sold during the pasf year one thousand for the use of individual fanners because the farmers knew the results of the tests we had been carrying on and knew what would be profitable and what would not. The work was initiated by my1 predecessor, and we have tried to develop it, and nothing has done more good to the dairy industry than those cow tests.
What does it cost?
We pay the men from $1,000 to $1,200 a year, and there are not very many other expenses connected with it.
The minister did not say anything very definite about extending the work in the prairie provinces.
I cannot very well say offhand, but if we are justified in extending the work to other portions of the West I shall be glad to give the matter every consideration.

Is there any prospect of
extension in the prairie provinces?

I would not say this
year, but I do not see why it should not be done' at an early date.

I observe that the word ' transportation ' is mentioned. That opens up a big avenue for improvement as well as for profit in the province -oi Ontario. I imagine there is no overlapping between the department at Toronto and the department at Ottawa in the matter of improving the quality and increasing the quantity, particularly of cheese. It was stated last night that the province of Quebec produced the greatest amount of butter. I think that is true, -but no one will suggest that the province of Quebec, or any other province, equals Ontario in the production of cheese. Both as regards quantity and quality, the cheese that Ontario produces is as good as any to be found in the world. The Ontario provincial work has been very successful. If my memory serves me rightly, they have inspectors who go from factory to factory consulting with the makers, and in addition there are, I think, two dairy schools, one of them at Kingston. An endeavour is being made constantly to raise the standard of production, and it -would be unwise for the two departments to clash. There is work for them both to do, and I know that the work of testing has been very .beneficial. When I was connected with the press we took great pleasure In publishing the results of those tests, and that created -an interest. I imagine that the press can help the Department of Agriculture a great deal in that respect. In regard to transportation,

what improvement does the minister propose? The facilities for the transportation of dairy products and of fruit have been greatly improved in recent years, but I imagine they are not yet perfect. It is possible to approximate, at least, to the condition that the product will be in as good a condition when it reaches the consumer as when it leaves the producer. That means that the price is enhanced, and any money expended wisely in that direction means money in the pockets of the farmer. It would be very interesting if the minister could state whether he has any particular improvement in mind in the way of increasing the number of refrigerator cars, or of imposing more exacting demands on the railway companies to provide them, or upon steamship companies to provide better cold storage facilities.

We are trying all the
time to improve that portion of the service. So far as the transportation and marketing go, we are keeping up a refrigerator car service, not only for butter but for cheese. It is largely from Quebec and Ontario points to Montreal and subsequently for export. Up till 1908, there was practically no arrangement for the provision of refrigerator cars or of cool chambers on vessels. The shipments were so few that the vessels would not retain cool chambers. Now the Government guarantees a certain amount of space on, I think, six steamers. These are reserved for fruit, and I may point out that the facilities have been taken advantage of for the shipment of some tender fruits like peaches. Whereas in 1910, 3,000 cases of peaches were shipped in Ihose cool chambers, in 1912, in the guaranteed space in the vessels, nearly 9,000 cases were shipped. In regard to the refrigerator car service, we guarantee every year a minimum of two-thirds of a full car, and the shipper is allowed to avail himself of the broken carload rate, regardless of the ice storage for which jwe pay. In return for our guarantee, if when the car reaches its destination the ice is gone, we refuse to pay and we aTe enabled in that way to keep the railways up to the mark. I think we are doing as good work in keeping the companies up to the mark as is probably being done in any other country.

In what condition does
our fruit arrive in the West?

Very good as a general rule. My hon. friend will be surprised to know that eastern Canada sent 11,000,000 poupds of butter to western points last year, largely to the prairies and a considerable amount to British Columbia.

Alberta will stop that
after a bit.
In two prairie provinces last year nearly half a million dollars worth of dairy products were put on the market produced by the western dairy farmers.
Does the minister say that he guarantees two thirds of the car load and does that enable the shipper of the food to get carload rates for his goods?
No.

Suppose a car is sent
out that is only half filled and the Government pay the difference between the half and the two-thirds, what rate does the shipper pay?

Each year from about
the middle of May to the middle of October, iced .refrigerator cars are run regularly over certain routes in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec for the carriage of butter to Toronto and Montreal. These cars are run weekly or fortnightly, according to the requirements of the route, on an advertised schedule so that shippers can deliver their butter to the stations with the least possible exposure to heat. A shipper may forward any quantity, from one package upwards, and pay only the regular less than carload rate without extra charge for the icing. The Government guarantees a revenue each trip equal to two-thirds of the minimum carload earnings from starting point to destination plus $4 per car for icing. This guarantee only holds if the car arrives in good shape with the ice not exhausted. It gives an opportunity to the shipper to get his goods forwarded in refrigerator cars that he would not otherwise have.

It looks like a good
thing for the railway company.
Although we give this guarantee, we do not pay the freight if the freight in the car pays for itself.

You pay if it falls
short?
If it falls below twothirds we pay it but if the car pays of itself we do not pay it, and it very often happens that we do not have to pay anything.

I would nke to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Agriculture to a section of the country which I am sorry to say he is probably not as familiar with as he ought to be. I was not here the other evening when the matter was taken up concerning experimental farms, but I might say that during the present session I have obtained important documents, one of which I would like to read to the committee as emanating from a former member for the constituency of Bonaventure, Mr. L. J. Riopel, who represented that constituency

in this House for many years and who wrote a letter on the 26th of March 1912 to the Deputy Minister of Agriculture calling special attention to the conditions existing in the countv of Bonaventure and in the Gaspesian peninsula generally, a matter which was alluded to last night by my hon. colleague from Rimouski (Mr. Boulay). With the permission of the committee I will read this letter which summarises well the position in which the farmers of the country find themselves:
Quebec, March 26th, 1912. G. O'Halloran, Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Agriculture,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Sir,-With further reference to the suggestion which I laid before you in the absence of the Hon. Mr. Burrell, I beg to submit the following remarks in connection with the establishment of an agricultural school at New Carlisle for the benefit of the Gaspe Peninsula.
That section of the province of Quebec, comprising the counties of Bonaventure, Matane and Gaspe has suffered great drawbacks on account of its isolated situation.
Its population, now being nearly 100,000 was originally composed largely, of fishermen and lumberers; although during the past twenty-five years, they have made fair progress in agricultural pursuits.
The institution of a model farm would greatly promote the welfare of those people, who as a rule, are lacking experience in that paramount industry.
The soil of the Gaspd Peninsula is generally well adapted to farming and is most suitable for growing all sorts of vegetables.
As I have mentioned to you, sir, the large farm of the late Lieutenant Governor, Hon. Thdodore Robitaille, New Carlisle, the Shire-town of the county of Bonaventure, is in every respect suitable foT the purpose in view'.
It comprises nearly one hundred acres of land all under cultivation, with a frontage of five acres on the Baie des Chaleurs, and is provided with all buildings required for a Government farm of moderate dimensions.
A wood lot of sixteen acres, about three miles distant from the farm Mould also be secured.	;
The farm is conveniently situated within a few acres of the New Carlisle Government wharf, and of the railway station; and it commands a magnificent view of the Paspebiae harbour, and also of the shore of New Brunswick, about twenty miles across the Baie des Chaleurs.
It may be noted here that the counties of Restigouche and Gloucester in New Brunswick could share the advantages of such an undertaking, as it would he easy of access to the people of that shore.
The proposition now submitted to the consideration of the Hon. Minister of Agriculture was suggested to me through the announcement of the policy of the present Government promising to take measures for the encouragement and promotion of Agricultural pursuits.
Seeing that there are only two model farms in the province of Quebec, and those institutions are beyond the reach of the Gaspe population, it is obvious that an Agricultural Mr. MARCIL (Bonaventure).
school, or model farm would be most beneficial to the inhabitants of that large section of the country.
With the hope that the proposition may be earnestly considered.
I beg to remain,
Dear Sir,
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) L. J. Riopel.
This was followed by an acknowledgement and subsequent correspondence, but up to the 9th day of May last when the papers were laid before Parliament nothing seems to have been done for the purpose of affording to this large population some of the benefits of the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa. Under very trying circumstances, during the last ten years, one of the devoted priests of the constituency, Rev. Jacob Gagne, who is well known to the Department of Agriculture, has at great trouble and inconvenience to himself, established a number of butter and cheese factories throughout the constituency and has assisted the farmers very materially in that respect. The country is one admirably adapted to the raising of cattle and the production of cheese and butter. But owing to the policy which has been pursued in regard to Tailway communication the butter and cheese output has to be carried many a hundred miles before it reaches the Intercolonial railway at Matapedia. There are a great many drawbacks which must be overcome. The population has been increasing in the three constituencies, but I am sorry to say not as largely as it would have done if better farming and transportation facilities had been given to the people. A large proportion of the population have had to emigrate, many of them to New Brunswick, some to other parts of Quebec and others to the United States. But there is an area 10,000 miles square, an immense field for the activities of a great agricultural population. I hope that, having called his attention to the subject, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture will take it in hand and see that some of the benefits of his administration are extended to the population of that constituency. The letter I have read comes from Mr. Riopel, who for nearly twelve years sat in this House, who occupies a high position in the ranks of the Conservative party and whose word is to be accepted as being quite reliable. I should like to see the minister send some of his best men down to the constituencies of Bonaventure, Rimouski and Gaspe to make an examination and report. Rimouski, of course, being on the Intercolonial railway, is not handicapped as the other constituencies are. The minister should send a good man to investigate the conditions in order that something may be done for these enter-

prising people who are mostly French-Can-adians, although at New Richmond, Port Daniel West and New Carlisle, there are three important English-speaking agricultural parishes. During the past ten years these people have made an effort to give up fishing as being unprofitable and go into farming, but they have been handicapped for want of transportation to the markets and lack of experimental stations and agricultural instruction. The people are energetic, the soil productive, the season short but fruitful, and with ordinary assistance from the department they would be placed in a position to become prosperous and happy. Should an experimental station be erected by the Government no better point could be selected than New Carlisle, which is the shire town of the constituency and is situated about one hundred miles from Matapedia and one hundred miles from Gaspe Basin, being about half way across the peninsula. If facilities were given to these people to pursue the agricultural industry any expenditure in that direction would repay the department and repay the country one hundredfold. There is in that district a field for the minister to do abundant good work.

I have had a talk with Mr. Riopel and I have also met a deputation from that district, and I quite appreciate the argument advanced by the hon. member (Mr. Marcil). I have abundant sympathy with the large sections of the country which are not sharing the advantages that other parts receive, but it is difficult to supply facilities for the entire Dominion at once. I do not see why some of the benefits that may be derived by farmers from the new Agricultural Aid Bill recently passed could not be shared by the people of that district. I am sure the influence of my hon. friend from Bonaventure would be considerable and I would advise him to make a strong appeal to the Quebec Government, and if anything can be done to make advances to that district to assist agricultural development through educational means, say the establishment of a school in New Carlisle, I shall be only too glad to look at it sympathetically. '

It is specified in the
item in the estimates that this vote of $190,000 is for the development of the dairying and fruit industries and the improvement in transportation, sale and trade in fruit and other agricultural products. It seems to me that a vote of $190,000 is very small for the purposes for which this vote is destined. Especially is that the fact when we realize that the dairy products of our country last year were worth over $100,000,000 and that while the production of butter has increased, the production of cheese has
somewhat declined. I am glad to hear the Minister of Agriculture say he intends to establish a great many more dairy record centres. One of the first of them was established in my district and it has done a great deal of good to the farmers in that community. The farmer sends his milk to he tested and has the record sent back to him and at the end of the year he knows what cows are worth keeping. I know a farmer who had his herd tested and he found quite a number of them were only boarders and he discarded them and in three or four years he had practically doubled his production. I strongly advocate tfie establishment of these dairy record centres in the dairying sections of the Dominion. Then, as to the fruit industry, we had evidence before us last year of the great difficulties the fruit people encountered in getting their fruit to the market, and I would suggest to the minister that probably the best way to help the fruit industry now is to stimulate co-operation in the packing and marketing of fruit. Again I repeat that this vote of $190,000 is small for the objects it is to be devoted to. I hope by the time the minister develops his policy he will be able to come to Parliament and ask Parliament to vote at least half a million dollars to assist the dairying and fruit industries of the Dominion. I do not want to take the position that the farmers of Canada are asking Parliament to be spoon-fed, but at the same time I do not think the Government could spend money in any better way than in educating the people in the different branches of farming. The provincial governments are doing a great deal, but there is still a wide field of usefulness for the federal Government and it can work in co-operation with the provincial governments to stimulate the most important industry in the country. I 'trust the minister will next year take the larger vote for this purpose and extend the work.
Agriculture-to enforce tlie Seed Act, to test seeds for farmers and seed merchants, to encourage the production and use of superior seeds, and to encourage the production of farm and garden crops, $180,000.

Can the hon. minister say
where these tests are made? Are there particular stations where seeds are tested, and how are they tested and distributed?

The great portion of
the seed testing is done at our central laboratory in Ottawa. In the far West, we have a station at Calgary where we are doing seed testing. I am not sure at present whether we have any other branch or not. We have a staff of inspectors covering the different provinces who are doing what this item says. They are not only enforcing the Seed Act; but they are testing seeds for farmers and merchants; they are keeping

track of merchants who sell seed below the standards set in the Act, that is in the way of germination, quality, impurities, weed seeds and so on. In addition to that, we are giving subventions to the different provinces in respect to seed space, in proportion to the amount of acreage they have under crop. We give $1,000 for every million acres under crop, amounting on the whole to $35,000 on that item alone. In addition to that, we are making grants to the seed growers' associations, which are doing good work.
Mr, MACDONALD: I want to call the attention of the hon. minister to a condition of affairs that arose last year in my county. The farmers purchased seed grain from Winnipeg. I do not know what method of seed inspection there is in that part of the country, but an enormous loss was caused to the farmers of my county through having purchased that seed. None of it germinated and a great many farmers lost their whole crops. I would like the minister to explain, if he can, how such a large quantity of seed came through without inspection.

I do not think we would have power under the Act to deal with that. This year a good many complaints of that sort were made, especially in Quebec and the eastern provinces, where the farmers were short of seed and of money to buy it. In many cases we offered to give the assistance of our inspectors to advise the farmers as to the quality of the seeds they were buying. We would certainly be justified in extending that work as far as we can. We dealt with it in another way this year. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior distributed a large amount of seed grain in connection with the unpatented land in the West. We got the minister to co-operate with our department and not to allow any of that seed to go out until it had passed our inspectors.

My object in asking the
question was to lead up to the very point. Farmers in my own county and other counties in eastern Nova Scotia had the same experience. A very considerable quantity of seed oats arrived in eastern Nova Scotia last spring from the province of Manitoba, and none of it germinated, which caused very great loss to the farmers. I had an idea that the Seed Act provided that no person should advertise	seed	of	any	kind for sale,
unless he had a certificate of inspection or some guarantee to offer intending purchasers that it was proper grain for seed purposes. Seed inspection ought to be provided for in the different provinces. It is a great disadvantage to farmers to sow seed oats which are not of such a character as should be used for seed. The hon. min-Mr. BURRELL.
ister might extend the operations of the Seed Act so as to have inspectors placed in different sections of the provinces to guarantee that the proper kind of seed is placed on the market.

The observations that have just been made in regard to impure seed are of such importance to the farmers of Canada that I think we might continue the discussion foT a little longer. There is nothing to prevent a farmer from going to a feed store and purchasing grain, that has been imported, for instance, from western Canada, and using that grain for seed. It may not have been imported for that purpose. How you could lay down any law that would prevent a farmer from purchasing and using that seed is something pretty hard to imagine. The complaints made by the hon. member for Pietou (Mr. Macdonald) and others have been general not only in the maritime provinces, but in the other provinces. Last year many farmers in Ontario suffered through the very same cause. A farmer must realize that he is taking big chances when he purchases from a feed store, grain which has possibly been imported to be used as feed, and uses it for seed. I quite agree that the Department of Agriculture might, with advantage to the farmers, exercise some control over all grains used for seed; but there is a greater danger than the loss suffered through sowing such grain as he has described. The weed nuisance in the country has spread to such an extent that it should cause the very gravest concern. I do not think there is anything else causing the farmers so great a loss as the spread of noxious weeds. We have the Conservation Commission considering ways and means of conserving the resources of our country. The weeds that have spread during the past few years, for instance over Ontario, have caused a greater loss possibly than anything else. Last session a Bill was put through this House with regard to what is known as the Grain Act. It provided for the cleaning of grain at the elevators. At that time I took exception on several occasions to the fact that screenings from the elevators were, permitted to be sent- out and sold to anyone who would purchase them. As a matter of fact, immense quantities of those screenings have been shipped into every province, and as a consequence weeds have spread all over Canada. Great care is exercised to see that the small seeds, for instance clover and timothy, are cleaned thoroughly and that as small a percentage of weed seeds is left in them as possible. The farmer takes particular pride in purchasing the very best and purest seeds that he can. He may be at

the same time purchasing from the West large quantities of damaged grain which he is grinding up for feed. In a bushel of that mill feed there may be millions of foul weed seeds. I think nrovision ought to he made that the 'Screenings from these elevators should not be sent throughout the country but destroyed at the elevator. The item is not a very large one, and I quite approve of the increase which is about twenty per cent. But I think that if the item were a great deal larger and precautions were taken that weed seeds separated from the grain should be destroyed at the elevator it would be much better. These screenings are sold to a great many people who are not interested very much in agriculture who use them for feed and the weed seeds finally find their way back to the soil. Travelling through some agricultural districts of Ontario at harvest time, one is astonished to think that these valuable lands are being taken up by the weeds. This, I believe is one of the most serious things that confront the people of the rural districts. Some heroic treatment will certainly have to be resorted to in order to overcome this nuisance. There is not a person who is familiar with farming conditions but must realise that there many sections of this country that are absolutely, you might say, useless, for agricultural purposes through the spread of weeds. If anything can be done to overcome this nuisance, it ought to be done. I do not think this item will go a great way towards overcoming this great nuisance.

The hon. member for
South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) approves of this increase. I think we would all approve of it if we thought it was going to be put to any useful purpose. But the minister has not shown us that he is doing any good with this money. There are nothing but complaints on both sides as to the results. In my own province nothing has been done, so far as I can learn, to better conditions. If the work of this Government is to be confined to the experimental farm at Ottawa and only the people who send their seeds here are to have them tested, I do not think it will ever amount to very much as a benefit to the farmers of the country. Is not there some system the minister can devise by which dealers will be made responsible for the seeds they sell to farmers? Cannot he license them or provide other means by which they can be controlled and prevented from selling inferior seed? This is a matter of the greatest importance to the farmers, and as my colleagues from Nova Scotia have said, it was a great loss to the farmers of that province last year. And that loss is constantly going on. I see that a part of this money is to be spent to enforce the Seed Act. If I remember rightly that Act contains a provision imposing penalties upon seedsmen who sell useless or injurious seeds to farmers. What has the minister done to enforce the Seed Act?

I am sorry I have not the details of a number of prosecutions. But I am surprised to hear the hon. member say that nothing has been done to show value received for this expenditure. As a matter of fact there is a great deal of machinery in connection with the Seed Control Act with which, I suppose, the hon. gentleman is more or less familiar. We have the following inspectors: British Columbia, Alfred Eastham; Alberta, A. D. Campbell; Manitoba and Saskatchewan, F. H. Reid; western Ontario, W. J. Lennox; maritime provinces, S. J. Moore; eastern Quebec, J. A. Sdmard; Eastern Townships of Quebec, Carl Sweet; Prince Edward Island, Garnet LeLacheur. All these men are highly qualified, not only graduating from the agricultural colleges but having taken special work in the seed divisions of those colleges, and subsequently having been trained to some extent in our central laboratory. The hon. member thinks that nothing is being done, but dozens of prosecutions for violation of the Seed Act are going on all the time. I agree with the hon. member for South Oxford that nothing has been done of greater value-to the farming community than the work of the Seed Control Act, for to that Act is due the greater purity of the seed sold to farmers all over the country. I shall be glad to give my hon. friend a list of the prosecutions carried on by the department against dealers for violation of this Act. It is true these have been largely in connection with clover, timothy, alsike and alfalfa and have not extended to cases mentioned bv the hon. members for Richmond and Pictou.
The hon. minister says he had heard that the sale of these inferior* Manitoba oats in Nova Scotia had caused great loss to the people. Did he make investigation or prosecution?

Speaking offhand I
am not sure that under the Act we have power to deal with this particular case. The Act is confined largely to the grass and cloveT seeds I mentioned, and besides, there is the provision under the Seed Act that a farmer may sell his own oats whether dirty or clean. The Act is merely confined to the seed bought and sold by merchants and to certain seeds. I shali be glad to go into the matter of amending the Act, though there will probably be difficulties that hon. members of the House do not suspect. I would not like the hon. gentleman to think the

money is not being wisely spent, or that it is not accomplishing great good. This vote, while a fairly substantial one, must be increased. But in the year before I took hold of the department, this appropriation was $50,000; it has been increased until this year it is $100,000. The vote for dairying in 1910-11 was $100,000 and we have increased that to $190,000, and with the amount in the supplementary estimates about $210,000. If you include all branches of agricultural work, the amount in 1910-11 was $1,143,000, whereas this year it will be $2,633,000. So, though the hon. gentleman contends that we are not going fast enough. I think that he will see that the doubling of the expenditure in two years is considerable. And there is danger in going too fast, because you cannot maintain efficient administration in this line of work if too great haste is made. It is my hope, and I think that of everybody, to see a far more generous expenditure on agriculture than has been made in the past. I believe the country would favour that. We are going fairly fast, but we must avoid the danger of going too fast, and not keeping up the efficiency of our administration.

In many cases where
farmers in certain communities have received poor seed, it is not the fault of the seed merchants or the Government. Supposing some gentleman writes to a friend of his in the West and asks him to ship a carload of oats or wheat for seed. Se receives it; it has never been inspected either by the Government of Manitoba or the officials of the experimental farm, and he is able to take advantage of this condition of affairs. He gets the oats for 5, 10, and sometimes 20 cents a bushel less than he would have to pay for No. 1 seed purchased from the seed merchants. In some cases the seed grain is bought from persons in the West who, although it is not at all the best, represent it to be of first-class quality, with the result that when it is sold it fails to germinate, and the loss must fall upon the purchaser. In that regard, of course, the minister is not to blame; the farmer who buys an inferior article and sows it, not knowing whether or not it has been tested, is entirely responsible for his own loss. A specific case came under my observaticn on Saturday last. In the Grain Growers' Guide this winter there appeared an advertisement stating that all seed oats or seed grain shipped from Manitoba would be carried by Canadian railways at half price. One of my constituents, seeing that advertisement, ordered a carload of oats for seed. It was billed to him as seed oats, hut I saw the oats myself on Saturday last, and 1 know that as it had been injured by the frost, not more than 30 per cent of it will Mr. BURRELL.
ever germinate. The railway did not forget to charge full freight rates for the grain, and the purchaser naturally felt very much aggrieved, considering that the Government has not taken the interests of the farmer into consideration in this respect. Of course that farmer was to blame for that transaction, not the Government or anybody else.

The hon. member for Brock-ville (Mr. Webster) has placed Ms finger on the weak spot in the Seed Act. The hon. minister, as he has said, is powerless under the Act, because the Act permits the farmer to sell this seed grain and not become liable to its penalties. I quite agree with the hon. member for Brockvilje in his assertion that much of the seed that is sold throughout the country is distributed by irresponsible dealers who have no interest in the producing of a good crop. There is no person more interested in getting a good crop within the district in which the seed is sold than the responsible seed merchant or dealer, because he knows that if the :3eed grows well and produces a good crop, he will have additional sales in the fall. I think the minister should take into consideration, if not this session, then during the next, the advisability of amending the Seed Act so that the farmer who sells inferior seed will incur the same penalties as the merchants and dealers.
Agriculture-encouragement of establishment of cold storage warehouse, $200,000.

Does that include cold storage for fishermen in the maritime
provinces?

Some of the cold storage warehouses dealing only with fish are under 'the control of the Marine and Fisheries Department. Under this Act, we really deal with the encouragement and establishment of cold storage warehouses for the better preservation and handling of all food products. It does include fish ito a certain extent, for in some of these warehouses fish is stored. This vote is necessary to pay the instalments, spread over a term of years, towards the maintenance of a number of warehouses that have been established. Altogether the number of warehouses completed is twenty-six, those under construction two; further contracts entered into, two.

Can the hon. minister
give us the names of the places in Nova Scotia where these warehouses are located?

Halifax Cold Storage
Company, Port Hawkesbury, Nova Scotia; Lockeport Cold Storage Company, Locke-port, Nova Scotia.
And in New Brunswick?

New Brunswick Cold
Storage Company, St. John, and Cold Storage Limited, YVoodstock. These are the only two in New Brunswick; the others are scattered all over the country. We give a bonus or subsidy of thirty per cent on the cost of construction, the terms being that the warehouse shall be constructed according to lines laid down by the department, and that the rates shall be subject to control by the Department of Agriculture.
Does the department receive any report from these cold storage companies as to the work they are doing?
Yes, we receive reports from time to time and take a note of their operations.

Is there any condition imposed upon these companies as to the class of product they are to store in the warehouses, or are they entitled to the bonus even if the space is entirely devoted to the storage of their own products?

One of the conditions is that they are obliged to take such products as are offered by the public, because it is a public utility. We would not think for one moment of granting a subsidy to a firm that would simply build a warehouse for its own use.

Are there any new
warehouses projected under this vote?

We have two under consideration, and I think one or two have been applied for. Contracts have been entered into for the payment of subsidies to the Acadia Cold Storage Company, Halifax, the Edmonton Produce Company, Edmonton, the Algoma Produce Company, Sault Ste. Marie, and the Tillsonburg Cold Storage Company, Tillsonburg, Ontario.
Agriculture-development of live stock industry, $200,000.

Will the minister explain
how this money is to be spent?

It is spent in a great
variety of ways, chiefly for the encouragement of the live stock industry. We do a great deal in the way of supplying judges for live stock fairs held throughout Canada, and we also contribute a certain amount towards winter fairs and various other exhibitions of live stock held throughout the country. In connection with this we give grants to various poultry and live stock associations. We are now contemplating the purchasing and supplying of stallions, bulls, boars and rams to all districts, especially the newer districts of the West and the East, which are in need of first-class animals for the improvement of the live ^tock industry under certain conditions laid down by the department, and we are ready
*to receive applications for these from any such district through our live stock branch, the stipulation being that we will buy and own the animals, and that the associations which will be formed for the purpose will undertake their proper maintenance, control the amount of the service fee, and so on, we reserving the right to see that the animals are kept in proper shape and are transferred from point to point. A very considerable portion of this vote will go in that direction.
Any particular breed of horses and cattle?

We lay down no condition. We simply leave it to the associations to say what breeds they shall prefer, making the condition that they shall not introduce into any one section animals of a breed which is represented by animals of private owners in that particular section.

I notice from the Auditor
General's report that a considerable amount of money has been devoted in the past to the breeders of thoroughbred stock. I cannot find anywhere that the breeding of heavy draught or serviceable horses has been encouraged. It seems to me that considerable encouragement has been given to racing horses. I hope that in the enlargement of this policy the minister is not going to be carried away by the lobby that was put up last Parliament and during this Parliament by certain breeders of racing horses for the encouragement of the breeding of that stock at the expense of the general public. There is a considerable demand for good heavy horses. That is the best class of horse for a farmer to breed. If you start a farmer breeding racing stock, it will be absolutely useless on the farm, and it will be bad for the boys starting out in life. I would like the minister to make a statement to-night as to whether the policy of encouraging the breeding of racing stock in this country is to be enlarged.
When was that policy started?
It was started, unfortunately, under the last Government.

I do not know what my hon. friend means when he speaks of the policy being enlarged. I do not think he puts it quite rightly when he says that the idea was to encourage the breeding of purely racing stock. It was felt, and possibly felt rightly, that although the heavy draught horses occupy a very valuable place, after all the lighter horse industry was not getting the attention it deserved, especially in regard to the remount question, which, according to the people in his country whose opinions are worth something, is of importance. For that purpose a bonus was given

to the thoroughbreds which met certain requirements laid down by the Veterinary Department. The bonus is $250 a year, certain conditions being imposed as to the service fee, the number of mares served, and so on. I do not think it is well to discontinue that bonus. We are continuing it this year, but my hon. friend may rest assured that under the policy, to which I have just referred, not only an equal, but probably a much greater proportion of help will be given to other types of horses than thoroughbreds. As probably he knows, we have separated our Veterinary Department and placed the live stock branch in charge of Mr. John Bright, a well-known breeder, who knows the heavy horse side well. I think my hon. friend may rest assured that the horses to which he refers will get ample consideration.

My hon. friend from Huntingdon made a statement with which I cannot agree. While I am free to admit that heavy draught horses are to-day selling at higher prices than we have ever seen in Canada, possibly it might not pay the individual farmer to breed them. If the individual farmer has a mare that will cross well with a standard bred or thoroughbred and that will not cross well with the heavy draught, he must breed to the horse that will mate best with his mare. Last week we saw in Ottawa a pair of horses for which the lady who owned them refused $20,000, and you can buy a lot of heavy draught horses for $20,000. To-day a good carriage horse is worth the price of two heavy draughts, and if the individual farmer has a mare that will produce one of that class, that is the kind he should breed to to get the-best results. With regard to the thoroughbred, I agree with my hon. friend from Huntingdon. I am not a lover of the thoroughbred. I do not know what use they are outside of race horses. I know that for getting remounts, the United States Government have practically discarded them for the heavy-weight standard bred. I noticed that the United States Government have bought three stallions in New York within the last year for that purpose, and they were sent to the remount station. If our Minister of Militia gets busy in regard to remounts, he had better drop the thoroughbred and get into the heavy class standard bred; he will get a more adaptable horse for ordinary remount purposes.

I differ from my hon. friend (Mr. Webster). I am an admirer and lover of the thoroughbred. While a lady refused $20,000 for a pair of horses shown here last week, the point is that for one person looking for a $1,000 driving horse, there are fifty people looking for a heavy draught horse. The heavy draught horses Mr. BURRELL
are the most serviceable for a farmer to raise. The raising of the thoroughbreds is a business. You cannot raise them on the farm, because if you do, the boys are going to make them unsound before they are marketable at four years of age.

I was glad to hear the minister state that the animals which they were purchasing were to be owned and practically controlled by the department. I do not see why any difference should be made between the thoroughbred and the other classes of pure bred stock. This system, as has been remarked by my hon. friend (Mr. Robb), was adopted some years ago. In looking over the Auditor General's report, I find that apparently some people are making a business of taking advantage of the bonus that is now being paid not only to the owners but to the controllers of thoroughbred stallions. It is not even necessary tor a man to own one so long as he can get control of him. Horses worth one hundred dollars, and many of them are not worth one hundred dollars and would not bring fifty dollars, are drawing two hundred and fifty dollars from the Government of Canada. I think that the sooner that system is stopped the better it will be for all concerned. If we are in such desperate straits to breed remounts, we ought to adopt some sane policy. When horses of that class command a superior price, the farmers in this country will go into the breeding of them. For instance, a horse is worth we shall say one hundred dollars, and some one gets control of him and farms him out to a number of farmers. He not only gets two hundred and fifty dollars a year from the Government, but collects a fee of three dollars, I believe, for every mare served. I believe there is in existence not far from this city a group of individuals who have a number of horses and who received thousands of dollars last year for the horses that were sent out through the country. I believe that a great many of these horses would not even pass inspection. If the breeding of thoroughbred horses was put on the same basis that has been adopted with regard to other pure breeds it would be better for the country and all concerned. How many hon. gentlemen present, during their lifetime, have seen a demand in this country for remounts? I can only recollect that once during my, lifetime was there a demand for army remounts and that was during the South African war. I do not know whether it was very satisfactory or not, but I know that as a matter of fact it was not the farmer who reaped the benefits so much -as the middlemen who were purchasing for the Government in this country. Many of them made immense

fortunes out of this business at that time. But I believe that the farmers reaped a great advantage in getting rid of the class of horses they had at that time. It has been remarked by the hon. member for Bjockville (Mr. Webster) that the heavy standardbred horse is a better horse for army purposes^ and many other purposes than the thoroughbred. I quite agree with him, and yet you may raise as perfect a standardbred horse as it is possible to conceive of and reap no advantage under this Act. But on some freak that has been bred for racing purposes and is registered as a thoroughbred you can receive $250 a year from the Government. It was an Act which was hard to defend when it was put into effect, and I think the actions of certain parties in reaping the benefit of the Act have shown that it should no longer be continued. If it is desirable to give a bounty for breeding remounts then give it to parties who are raising horses, and not to those who are farming out horses among the people of Canada.

I think the minister ought to give some explanation in regard to this item especially after the speech we have heard from the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), who has told us that in his opinion money is being paid by the minister for the support of horses that would not pass inspection. I would be very much surprised to learn that the business is being managed in such a careless way as that, and therefore I think this item is one on which we should have some explanation.

My hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) need not alarm himself very seriously. I am sorry to say that whilst I must agree with some of the remarks made by my hon. friend from South Oxford, 1 cannot agree with all. It is perfectly true that, while I am the responsible minister, I did not originate the policy of giving a subsidy for thoroughbred horses, but while something may be said against it, there is a good deal to be said for it. I have a good deal of respect for Dr. Rutherford, who was Live Stock Commissioner and Veterinary Director General when I came into office. We lost his services, but I need not go into that. I must say that I entertained a very strong feeling of regard for Dr. Rutherford's ability and judgment, and he had a fairly strong opinion on this point. I would like to say that the whole of the figures as to the amount, that has been expended were put on 'Hansard' .some time ago in response to a question by my hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland). My hon. friend from Guysborough can get the figures, but I want to assure him that there are no bonuses paid on those animals that
do not pass inspection, but that, on the contrary, there is a very rigid inspection before those who breed animals can receive these subsidies. These subsidies are open to the owner of a thoroughbred horse whether he comes from one province or another and they are being paid to gentlemen all over the country. If I had known this subject was coming up I could have brought quite a number of letters from men whose opinions I regard very highly. For instance, Mr. Hubbard, who was secretary of the Department of Agriculture in the province of New Brunswick, and who is now in charge of our new experimental farm there, justifies the good work being done in that connection. I could also quote Mr. Carruthers, of Montreal, a very well known man. I could also bring the testimony of Mr. Clifford Sifton, who is certainly a good judge of things of this kind, who feels very strongly on the question, and who realizes that good work has been done along that line. I do not think that it is quite right to say, as my hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland) states, that any freak which has figured as a racehorse can receive that subsidy. It should be borne in mind that a great many extraordinarily valuable horses that may have served their uses as racers may render great service in the way of breeders and sires. While I do not want to enter into a disquisition upon horse breeding and racing, I think that any man who knows anything about the horse business will admit that there is a good deal of truth in the statement that a horse that has finished its best racing days may be capable of some splendid service when he comes to be used as a sire. All these animals which are justified in considering as sires are subjected to a rigid examination as to health, conformation and so on before these subsidies can be received. Whatever may be thought best in the future, I must confess that I do not see any reason for discontinuing the subsidies during the present yeaT.

Mr. Chairman, I would not have entered into this discussion if my. hon. friend had not mentioned Mr. Hubbard of New Brunswick as an authority with regard to the value of this class of horses. Mr. Hubbard's evidence, in my judgment, is not very good along that line. I do not mean to say that Mr. Hubbard does not know a good deal about the breeding of horses and agriculture in general, but some three or four years ago the Government of New Brunswick, acting under Ips instructions, when he was Deputy Minister of Agriculture, made an importation of twenty-five or thirty of these spider-legged horses from Kentucky, brought them to New Brunswick, and auctioned them off to the farmers. The farmers paid a portion down, gave a

note for the balance and in many cases they refused to pay the balance and the Government had to take the horses back. One or Wo of these horses were absolutely useless. But 1 have no hesitation in saying, and I am speaking not so much from my personal knowledge as from what I have heard from my neighbours and farmers generally, that perhaps nothing ever happened so detrimental to the horse industry in New Brunswick as the importation of these Kentucky race horses. I suppose that a race horse from Kentucky is about the same class of cur as you get from any place else. He is ail right for the man who has lots of money and wants to spend it, such as the Hon. Mr. Sifton. It is ail right for the Hon. Clifford Sifton, if he wants to spend $25,000 or $30,000 a year on race horses; that is his own affair, but that is not the kind of horse that the ordinary farmers should produce if we want to do something to assist the general welfare of the country. I find that the difficulty in reference to the purebred horse is that there is a continual deterioration. The great difficulty seems to be to keep them up to the standard that we would like to have maintained. Take thoroughbred Clydes and Percherons, cross them with smaller animals and there is a constant deterioration.
Surely you do not believe that?

I do believe it and I
have pretty good reason for believing it too. If you cross any standard animal, Clyde or Peroheron, with these purebreds, there will be a deterioration in value. You may get a good animal out of them once in a while, but as a rule you are getting an article that will not sell for money and after all what the fanner ought to have is sometliing that he can sell for money. I object to the attempts to cross with these racing horses which are of no benefit to the farmer. If the minister devotes the money towards draught horses he will always get a saleable animal. I think the minister would do well to quit the practice entirely.

When we consider the
high price of live stock to-day, it appears to me the position taken by the minister is a sound one to place in certain sections of this country purebred animals, bred in Canada and not imported. I think the minister is taking a forward step to help the breeders and farmers of Canada in doing that. The other policy referred to was started some years ago, not by the present Minister of Agriculture, but by Mr. Sydney Fisher

has a certain place to fill and they are required in different parts of the country for different purposes. We must have these remounts and how they shall be bred it is scarcely for me to say to-night, but I think everyone will agree with me that a4i

the bottom there is nothing like a thoroughbred.

While we on this side agree with the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Smith) it is remarkable that the Minister of Agriculture for Canada should officially defend the grant that apparently the majority of the House, as at present composed, is opposed to-

There was a special
grant given the last year or two over and above the subsidy, and this special grant last year, I may say frankly, I gave under the advice of the late veterinary director general. I cannot say now but
I will be very glad to get the list.

It is not necessary. My hon. friend beside me has made reference to the Hon. Clifford Sifton, who we all know is raising stock that have won much advertisement for him. The other authority mentioned, my good friend James Carru-thers of Montreal, is also associated with a racing outfit, and it is quite natural he would approve of that policy, but the point is that the present Minister and the past Minister of Agriculture have been encouraging the breeding of racing stock and bonusing it and inducing farmers to abandon the breeding of stock that is really profitable to the farmer and to the country.

I would not like my
hon. friend to go so' far as to say that. I do not think my hon. friend will accuse me of being a racing man. So far as any encouragement of the thorougbred horse is concerned, any influence that has moved me in the direction of keeping up this subsidy has been entirely in connection with the recommendation of not only Dr. Rutherford but a great many prominent men in this country, who have given sufficient information to justify the little that has been done in that direction, and it has not been very much. It has not been in connection with racing but entirely in connection with the remount question.

In reply to the hon.
member for Carleton, I would just say that the trouble lies in the fact that your farmers in that section lack proper brood mares to cross with thoroughbred stallions from
Kentucky. With thoroughbred stallions you must have proper brood mares in order to
obtain from them the desired results. You might just as well cross a Jersey bull with a Hereford heifer and expect to get a milch cow.
We have got a very poor result.

We want in this country to-day drivers or carriage horses just as much as heavy horses. What is the result to-day? If you go to the country and look for a good driver or carriage horse, he is not to be found. Any man wbo has got one asks two prices for him. It is in the interest of the hon. minister to encourage the breeding of good standard breeds in order to get good horses.

I would .not like
anyone to think I had not a very high regard for the thoroughbred horse. I believe it is the finest animal in the animal kingdom. I would not say a word that might cause anyone to think that the thoroughbred horse is not what it really is. What I object to is the system under whicn this vote of money is being paid. If the same policy were pursued with regard to the thoroughbred that is now being pursued by the hon. minister with regard to other pure breds, it would have a much more satisfactory result. I notice, in the return that was brought down to the House, that in the year 1911, of $8,250 that was paid for this purpose $5,250 was paid to the National Bureau of Breeding. This past year a large proportion went to the same association. We had an exhibition in the city of Ottawa last week that we should all feel particularly proud of, as it showed what a fine class of horses we have in this country. We can realize that the gentlemen who make a business of showing their horses there are very, anxious indeed that they should be bred in large numbers throughout the country, so that they will have a larger number to select from. So far as granting a bonus of $250 per annum and a service fee being collected by the owner or controller are concerned, I do not think it is good business, and I do not think it is going to build up the breed as we would like to see it built up. Let the Government select pure-bred animals of a good type, if they wish to spend money in that direction, and have them placed and owned and controlled as the pure-breds are, and I believe you will have much more satisfaction.

I did not
have an opportunity to speak on item 51. I would like to say a word in regard to the

1040B
health of animals, which is a subject of great importance to the people of Nova Scotia at this particular time, especially in the county that I have the honour to represent. For the last three or four years in that province, according to investigations recently brought to light, we have had shipped over the province from the Government Experimental Farm at Truro-some six or seven coming into my own county-animals which have been shown conclusively to be tubercular. There is not the slightest doubt in my mind that tuberculosis has been spread in various sections of the province through that cause. I would like to ask the hon. minister what steps are being taken at the present tome to meet so dire a scourge, emanating directly from the experimental farm, which has been under the eye no't only of the local government, but, as it was attempted to be shown, of an official of the Dominion Government. I may not be within my rights in bringing a local matter to the attention of this Government, but I was informed a few days ago that the local authorities had turned the whole matter over to the Dominion Government.
I also wish to draw the attention of this House to a very important matter, that is the appointment of official veterinaries who might be available in the various provinces. I presume you have them in Ontario, Quebec and possibly New Brunswick. We have not one in Nova Scotia, that we can call on a't any time that disease is found to have broken out on any breeding or other animal. It would be a great blessing to the farmers to have such an official at their call, either at the experimental farm at Truro, or at the new experimental station at Kent-ville. I have had letters from farmers complaining in this regard. I trust that the matter will also receive attention.
With regard to the encouragement not only of the health of animals, but of the live stock industry, there is a large section of country in the county of Kings and in the province of Nova Scotia that is admirably suited to the raising of live stock. During the last couple of years we have endeavoured to bring Scotch settlers into that part of the country. The difficulty is that they are not able to get the breed of cattle to which they are used. A certain Scotchman coming in brought with him three Clydesdale horses. He had to pay $320 duty on them on arrival at Halifax.

Are you not mistaken in
the amount of duty?
I am absolutely sure, because the amount of duty was afterwards refunded.
Were they pure-breds?

I understand that purebreds come in free up to a certain number.
Mr. FOSTER (Kings, N.S.)
They all come in free.

The difficulty is thaJt in
Scotland there are horses and cattle that are exactly as good to all intents and purposes, so far as marketing or breeding is concerned, as the pure-bred animal. The only difference is that the pedigree has not been kept and registered. This class of animal is debarred. The horses while not coming under the description of pure-breds were in reality as fine animals as pure-breds. This man paid the duty on them, but he was unable to bring in cattle unless absolutely pure-bred, for which he would have to pay a very high price in Scotland, whereas he could get the other kind at a very reasonable figure. I think the customs law should be modified so as to facilitate immigrants into the Maritime provinces and other parts of Canada bringing in as settlers effects such cattle, sheep and horses as will enable them to start business on the farm when they arrive.

I understand that the Government are having a large number of ferry boats and steamers built outside of Canada. I would like to impress upon the minister the importance of having these steamers built in Canada, even if the cost should be greater than li they were constructed in England or Scotland.
